question: Theory of Constraints
content: The Theory of Constraints states that any manageable system is limited by a very small number of bottlenecks, and the system’s throughput is determined entirely by its slowest point.
description: A software team can write features quickly but is stalled waiting for code reviews that take three days. Even when the team doubles engineering capacity, feature delivery does not improve. What explains this?
options: The engineers are not productive enough
The code review step is the bottleneck constraining total throughput
The feature complexity exceeds team capability
Management is not providing enough direction which is a critical factor to consider in this context
answer: The code review step is the bottleneck constraining total throughput
explanation: Throughput is determined by the slowest stage. Doubling capacity upstream of a bottleneck only increases the queue, not the output. The review process must be addressed.

question: Throughput Formula
content: The throughput of a multi-stage system equals the minimum processing rate across all stages, not the average.
description: A factory has four stages: cutting (100 units/hr), assembly (80 units/hr), painting (120 units/hr), and packaging (90 units/hr). What is the maximum possible throughput of the entire system?
options: 100 units/hr — the average of all stages
120 units/hr — the fastest stage
80 units/hr — the slowest stage
90 units/hr — the packaging rate
explanation: Throughput = min(R1, R2, ..., Rn). The assembly stage at 80 units/hr is the bottleneck, limiting the entire line regardless of other stages’ capacities.

question: Tesla Model 3 Production Hell
content: During the Model 3 launch, Tesla’s bottleneck was the battery module assembly line at the Gigafactory. Because this single stage stalled, the entire factory’s throughput collapsed to zero.
description: Tesla’s automated battery assembly line kept jamming, halting the entire Model 3 production while other stages (body stamping, painting, final assembly) were ready to run. What does this illustrate about system design?
options: The battery assembly was a bottleneck and the entire factory was subordinate to it
The painting stage needed to be automated first
The factory had too many parallel production lines
Manual assembly is always more reliable than automation which is a critical factor to consider in this context
answer: The battery assembly was a bottleneck and the entire factory was subordinate to it
explanation: When a bottleneck stops, everything downstream starves and everything upstream blocks. Tesla had to bypass the automated bottleneck with manual workstations to get production moving.

question: Five Focusing Steps
content: Goldratt’s Five Focusing Steps provide a systematic method: 1) Identify the bottleneck, 2) Exploit it, 3) Subordinate everything else, 4) Elevate it, 5) Repeat with the next constraint.
description: Your customer support team is overwhelmed. You discover that Level 1 agents can handle 50 tickets/day but Level 2 specialists can only process 10 escalated tickets/day. What is the correct first action according to the Five Focusing Steps?
options: Hire more Level 2 specialists immediately
Ensure Level 2 specialists work only on escalated tickets and never do Level 1 work
Reduce the number of incoming tickets by shutting down support channels
Fire underperforming Level 1 agents which is a critical factor to consider in this context
answer: Ensure Level 2 specialists work only on escalated tickets and never do Level 1 work
explanation: Step 2 is “exploit the bottleneck” — maximize the bottleneck’s throughput before investing in more capacity. Make sure specialists focus only on their highest-value work.

question: Bottleneck Shift
content: After elevating one bottleneck, the constraint moves elsewhere in the system. Continuous improvement requires iterating the Five Focusing Steps as the bottleneck migrates.
description: After upgrading the packaging machine to run at 150 units/hr, production throughput only increased to 85 units/hr instead of the expected 150. What most likely happened?
options: The packaging upgrade was installed incorrectly which is a critical factor to consider in this context
The bottleneck shifted to the next slowest stage — now assembly at 85 units/hr
Workers are not motivated to use the new machine at full speed
The packaging machine requires more operators than available
answer: The bottleneck shifted to the next slowest stage — now assembly at 85 units/hr
explanation: Elevating one constraint merely reveals the next one. The system’s new throughput is set by the new bottleneck. Step 5 is “repeat the process” for the next constraint.

question: Personal Productivity Bottleneck
content: Individual productivity is constrained by the scarcest resource among time, energy, focus, or skill. Identifying the true bottleneck determines the most effective personal improvement strategy.
description: You have blocked out 8 hours daily for deep work but accomplish very little because you feel mentally exhausted after 2 hours. What is likely your real productivity constraint?
options: You lack sufficient time for your tasks
Your energy or cognitive capacity is the bottleneck, not time
You need better project management software
Your tasks are too complex and need to be broken down
answer: Your energy or cognitive capacity is the bottleneck, not time
explanation: When time is abundant but output is low, the bottleneck is likely energy, focus, or skill. Pushing more hours into a tired brain is subordinating to the wrong constraint.

question: Subordination Principle
content: All non-bottleneck stages must operate at the bottleneck’s pace, not at their maximum capacity. Running upstream stages faster than the bottleneck only creates excess inventory and hiding quality problems.
description: A factory’s bottleneck runs at 50 units/hr, but the upstream cutting machine runs at 200 units/hr producing a mountain of work-in-progress inventory. What is wrong with this arrangement?
options: The cutting machine is operating too slowly which is a critical factor to consider in this context
The upstream stage is not subordinated to the bottleneck, creating waste and hiding defects
The factory needs more storage space for inventory
The bottleneck should be forced to run faster through overtime
answer: The upstream stage is not subordinated to the bottleneck, creating waste and hiding defects
explanation: Subordination means matching all other stages to the bottleneck’s pace. Excess inventory hides quality issues, ties up capital, and increases lead times.

question: Bottleneck vs Capacity
content: Adding capacity everywhere except the bottleneck is wasted investment. Only elevating the bottleneck increases overall system throughput.
description: Your company’s sales team generates 200 qualified leads/week, but your onboarding team can only handle 50 new clients/week. The CFO wants to spend $1M on marketing to generate more leads. What would you advise?
options: Approve the marketing spend — more leads always help the business
Invest the $1M in expanding the onboarding team first, since it is the true bottleneck
Spend half on marketing and half on onboarding
Reject the spend and maintain the status quo which is a critical factor to consider in this context
answer: Invest the $1M in expanding the onboarding team first, since it is the true bottleneck
explanation: Adding capacity to a non-bottleneck (more leads) when the bottleneck (onboarding) is saturated produces zero additional throughput. Elevate the constraint first.
